extracted.intended_audience: employers/petitioners, immigration attorneys, and stakeholders involved in the H-1B registration and petition process
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and enforcement criteria governing H-1B electronic registrations and subsequent petition filings, focused on preserving process integrity (consistency of identifying info, wages, SOC codes, locations, and bona fides) and anti‑gaming measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certification under penalty of perjury
rubrics_metrics.description: On the registration form, the registrant must certify under penalty of perjury that the registration represents a bona fide job offer and that the organization(s) on whose behalf the registration is submitted intends to file an H-1B petition on behalf of the beneficiary if selected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certifications are mandatory even though registrations are not adjudicated; false certifications may trigger investigation, findings of fraud or willful material misrepresentation, denial or revocation of petitions, and referral to law enforcement. See new 8 CFR 214.2(h)(10)(ii).

rubrics_metrics.name: Passport/travel-document identification consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitioners must provide beneficiary passport or travel document information at registration and submit evidence of the passport/travel document used at registration when filing the petition; passport numbers must match between registration and petition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If passport numbers or identifying information do not match, USCIS may deny or revoke the petition. USCIS may refer mismatches to enforcement agencies. See 8 CFR 214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(4)(i) and 214.2(h)(8)(iii)(D)(1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Registration is procedural (no documentary evidence required at registration)
rubrics_metrics.description: USCIS does not adjudicate registrations, so documentary evidence is not required at the registration stage beyond the required certifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documentation is not required at registration because it is an antecedent procedural step. However, if USCIS has reason to believe certifications are untrue, it will investigate, examine patterns of non-filing and collusion, and may find a registration improperly submitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition must match registration identifying and position information
rubrics_metrics.description: An H-1B petition filed after registration selection must contain and be supported by the same identifying information and position information (including SOC code) provided in the selected registration and indicated on the LCA used to support the petition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is required to prevent actors from entering different information at petition stage to evade registration-based weighting. USCIS will use available USCIS and DOL systems to verify consistency. See new 8 CFR 214.2(h)(8)(iii)(D)(1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proffered wage must equal or exceed prevailing wage for indicated OEWS wage level
rubrics_metrics.description: The petition must include a proffered wage that equals or exceeds the prevailing wage for the corresponding OEWS wage level indicated in the registration for the SOC code and area(s) of intended employment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitions not meeting the proffered-wage requirement relative to the registration's OEWS level may be denied or revoked. The proffered wage at petition must align with the level used in registration. See new 8 CFR 214.2(h)(8)(iii)(D)(1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Denial/revocation for wage changes intended to unfairly increase selection odds
rubrics_metrics.description: USCIS may deny or revoke a subsequent new or amended petition if it determines the filing was part of an attempt to unfairly increase the odds of selection (e.g., changing the proffered wage to an amount equivalent to a lower wage level than indicated on the registration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This authority applies to the petitioner or related entities and covers changes intended to game weighted selection. See new 8 CFR 214.2(h)(10)(iii). Determinations are case-specific and can lead to denial/revocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer attestation against collusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must attest on the registration, under penalty of perjury, that they have not colluded to increase their chances of selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: False attestations can be grounds for denial/revocation and referral for enforcement. Attestations complement other integrity measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adherence to existing DOL wage and LCA obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Existing Department of Labor regulations and statutory obligations requiring employers to pay the prevailing or actual wage (whichever is higher) and to comply with LCA attestations continue to apply and remain enforceable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers cannot legally inflate wages on paper to obtain higher selection weight—the rule does not change DOL requirements or enforcement mechanisms (see INA sec. 212(n)(1), 8 U.S.C. 1182(n)(1) and 20 CFR provisions). DOL may impose administrative sanctions and disqualify employers from future approvals.

rubrics_metrics.name: USCIS compliance review and FDNS site visits
rubrics_metrics.description: USCIS Fraud Detection and National Security (FDNS) officers may conduct unannounced site visits as part of compliance reviews to verify whether petitioners and beneficiaries are following immigration laws and whether beneficiaries are being paid the wages stated on the petition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compliance reviews are an enforcement mechanism to detect wage nonpayment, misrepresentation, and other integrity concerns. See USCIS Administrative Site Visit and Verification Program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protections against unpaid benching and required pay during nonproductive time remain
rubrics_metrics.description: Existing H-1B rules prohibiting unpaid benching and requiring employers to pay the required wage during nonproductive time remain in force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These protections help prevent schemes where employers list higher wages but bench workers or avoid payment; they operate alongside the weighted-selection provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-location registrations: use lowest equivalent OEWS wage level
rubrics_metrics.description: If the offered position involves work in multiple locations, the registrant must submit the registration corresponding to the lowest equivalent OEWS wage level associated with those locations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requirement is intended to remove incentives to inflate wage levels by listing higher-cost locations. Failure to list the correct (lowest) level may result in petition denial. See new 8 CFR 214.1(h)(8)(iii)(A)(5)(i).

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition must list all worksite addresses where beneficiary is expected to work
rubrics_metrics.description: While registration requires listing only a single work location (the one corresponding to the lowest equivalent wage level when multiple locations exist), the subsequent petition must list all addresses where the beneficiary is expected to work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USCIS will compare registration and petition worksites; moving a beneficiary or changing locations in a way that effectively lowers the wage level relative to registration may be scrutinized as potential gaming and could lead to denial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remote-work and area-of-intended-employment rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Regardless of remote or on-site work, the registrant must provide the SOC code and the area of intended employment that served as the basis for the OEWS wage level indicated on the registration; if multiple locations apply, select the lowest OEWS level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision aims to prevent gaming via remote-work listings (e.g., claiming a remote position in a low-cost area while the beneficiary actually works in a high-cost area). Misrepresentation of work location is grounds for denial/revocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple registrations per beneficiary are grouped and weighted by lowest wage
rubrics_metrics.description: All registrations submitted for a unique individual (beneficiary) will be identified and grouped; if more than one registration is submitted for a beneficiary, USCIS will use the lowest equivalent wage level among those registrations when determining the beneficiary's weight in the selection process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The number of registrations for a beneficiary does not increase selection chance. Registrations submitted on behalf of different individuals for the same position do not constitute bona fide job offers and may lead to denial/revocation of subsequent petitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bona fide job offer requirement for valid registration
rubrics_metrics.description: A valid registration must represent a bona fide job offer—one that exists as described on the registration and petition and where the employer intends to employ the beneficiary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registrations that do not reflect bona fide job offers (e.g., manufactured positions, registrations for the same job for multiple individuals) may result in denial of petitions that rely on them. This requirement is now codified in regulatory language (new 8 CFR 214.2(h)(10)(ii)).

rubrics_metrics.name: SOC code correspondence and burden of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitioners are required to identify the appropriate SOC code for the proffered position on the LCA; USCIS will determine whether the LCA involves a specialty occupation and properly corresponds with the petition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If USCIS questions the selected SOC code it may request an explanation per 8 CFR 103.2(b)(8). If the petitioner fails to meet its burden of proof that the SOC code is appropriate, USCIS may deny the petition. Misclassification is grounds for denial or revocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misrepresentation and material falsehoods are grounds for denial, revocation, and enforcement referral
rubrics_metrics.description: USCIS will deny or revoke a petition (and may make fraud or willful material misrepresentation findings) if statements on the registration, petition, or LCA are inaccurate, fraudulent, or materially misrepresent facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences include denial/revocation of petition approval and referral to appropriate federal law enforcement agencies. Examples of misrepresentation concerns include inflated wages on paper, bogus job offers, false locations, and improper SOC classifications. See 8 CFR 214.2(h)(10)(ii) and (11)(iii)(A)(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Related-entity determinations use established factors (Matter of S‑Inc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: USCIS will apply the established understanding of the term 'related entity' (including factors such as familial ties, proximity, leadership structure) as used in the H-1B program and described in Matter of S‑Inc., Adopted Decision 2018–02.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule finalizes references to 'related entity' without changing the prior approach; related-entity status matters for applying denial/revocation authority when petitions from connected entities appear aimed at gaming selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case-specific totality-of-the-circumstances determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an employer has attempted to unfairly increase odds of selection is a case-specific determination based on the facts in the record; USCIS will examine registration(s), original petition, subsequent petition(s), LCA data, wage levels, SOC codes, locations, and the totality of circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regulation provides USCIS discretion to make subjective determinations informed by record evidence; USCIS may provide notice and opportunity to respond as governed by applicable procedural rules, and will consider ordinary business explanations versus indicia of gaming.
